newsitem.title: USA: New York utilities Brooklyn Union, Lilco to merge.
newsitem.headline: New York utilities Brooklyn Union, Lilco to merge.

text.p: Brooklyn Union Gas Co. and Long Island Lighting Co. (Lilco) said Sunday they agreed to merge in a stock deal that would create a $4 billion electric and gas company.

Under the deal, Brooklyn Union shareholders would get one share of the company to be formed from the merger for each share they now hold, and Lilco shareholders would receive 0.803 shares of the new company.

Brooklyn Union provides natural gas service to the New York City boroughs of Brooklyn, Queens and Staten Island. Lilco provides power and gas to the eastern Long Island counties of Nassau and Suffolk as well as parts of Queens.
The two companies serve a total of 2.2 million customers.

The deal has been seen as key to lowering electric rates on New York's Long Island, which has some of the highest rates in the nation, due mostly to Lilco's massive debt for the Shoreham nuclear power plant, which never opened.
Lilco shareholders would own about 66 percent of the new company, and Brooklyn Union shareholders would own about 34 percent. The deal was structured as a pooling of interest.
The combined value of the two companies at Friday's stock prices is $4 billion. Their annual revenues are about $4.5 billion, the companies said.
The companies said that upon completion of the merger, William Catacosinos, chariman eand chief executive officer of Lilco, will be chairman and chief executive of the new holding company.

Robert Catell, chairman and chief executive of Brooklyn Union, will be president and chief operating officer. One year after closing, Catell will succeed Catacosinos as CEO, with Catacosinos continuing as chairman.

"The consolidation of our neighbouring companies will result in synergy savings in excesss of $1 billion over 10 years, which will provide rate reductions to customers," Catacosinos said in a statement.
For Brooklyn Union, the merger offers access to a big new market where natural gas plays a minor role now.

"Our combination with Lilco opens up the substantial Long Island market for Brooklyn Union," Catell said in a statement. "This market is particularly attractive because there is a low penetration of gas as a percent of the total energy provision in that region."
